docs.title: MirrorKit
docs.text:
Live mirrors for Chivalry 2 Unchained maps. Reflections show you, other players and the room; facing mirrors can form a tunnel, and there are cheap shiny surfaces and breakable mirror tiles. MirrorKit is a library: it adds no map by itself, and maps that use it need it installed.

Version 1.0.0. Built with ArgonSDK (Unreal Engine 4.25). The MirrorLab map shows every mirror type; MirrorMaze is a full mirror maze built with it.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• True reflections. You see your own full body in first person (moving legs, head, the weapon in your hand), other players and the room, with nothing behind the mirror leaking in.
  • Partner tunnels. Two facing mirrors set as partners show a reflection inside a reflection. With InfiniteTail on, the tunnel keeps going.
  • Styles and bodies. Every mirror has a Style (True, Floor, Funhouse) and a Body (Full body, Head only, Stretch head, Headless, Ghost).
  • Breakable tiles and cheap surfaces. Tiles break and can be walked through; baked mirror materials cost almost nothing.
  • Scales to the player. Each reflection is sized to the part of the screen it covers, so small and distant mirrors cost less. Quality presets and a shared capture budget keep mirror-heavy maps playable.
  • Players and servers choose. Players can lower or raise the quality, servers can set it for everyone or cap it, and maps keep working without the options.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Copy MirrorKit.pak and the map's own PAK into Chivalry 2/TBL/Content/Paks/, then launch through the Unchained Launcher. Server hosts need both files on the server too. The server itself renders no mirrors.

Without MirrorKit.pak a map that uses it still loads, but its mirrors are missing.

docs.title: Mirror quality
docs.text:
Every map ships with mirror settings chosen by its maker. You can raise or lower them for your own game, and server hosts can set them for everyone.

For your own game: add a launch option under Settings › Advanced Settings › CLI Arguments in the Unchained Launcher, for example:

-MirrorQuality=Low

For a server, or when playing offline: put it in the map's Options box in the Unchained main menu, with a ? instead of a -:

?MirrorQuality=High

Preset For Off No live reflections; mirrors show dark glass Low Weaker PCs: softer, slower reflections Medium A middle ground High The settings tuned for mirror-heavy maps Ultra Strong PCs: full resolution, the nearest mirrors update every frame Omega Ultra plus partner tunnels, the most expensive

Only the tunnels: -MirrorPartners=1 (or ?MirrorPartners=1) turns partner tunnels on without changing anything else; 0 turns them off. A server can forbid them with ?MirrorNoPartners.

Partners on Partners off

Jitter at high uncapped FPS: if reflections look slightly jittery when you move sideways along a mirrored wall (usually above about 200 FPS), add -MirrorFocusRate=1000. The mirrors nearest you then update every frame. It costs about 10 % FPS on a mirror-heavy map; at a frame cap of 144 or lower you do not need it.

If you choose nothing, mirrors use the map's settings, or the server's if the host set any. Single values (resolution, update rate, distance and more) and a server cap are also available: every quality option.

docs.title: Making a map with mirrors
docs.text:
1. Copy the Content of MirrorKit_Source.zip to ArgonSDK/Content/Mods/MirrorKit/ (this exact folder: the shared PAK loads the assets under these names).
  2. Drag BP_CaptureMirror (or a preset) into your level, face its +X axis out of the wall, and size it with the actor scale (Y and Z × 100 = width and height in cm).
  3. Keep 4 cm clear behind the face (5 cm with a partner); the orange box shows the space when the mirror is selected.

It works with no other setup. The map-making guide covers spacing, packaging your map without the kit's files, settings for many mirrors at once, the capture budget, tiles and every setting.

docs.title: Choose the look
docs.text:
Setting Choices Style True: a true reflection (default). Floor: sharper for large floor mirrors seen from above. Funhouse: magnified carnival look with gaps at the edges Body How your own reflection looks: Full body (default), Head only, Stretch head (stretches as you look up and down), Headless, Ghost (invisible body, floating weapons) Partner The facing mirror for a tunnel. Both mirrors name each other; leave it empty for a normal mirror

Ready-made presets: BP_Mirror_Funhouse, BP_Mirror_Headless, BP_Mirror_StretchHead (renders at full resolution, since the effect needs detail) and BP_Mirror_Ghost. Every setting can still be changed on any placed mirror.

Body effects are per viewer: a ghost or headless mirror changes only your own reflection as you see it; other players see you normally.

docs.title: Other pieces
docs.text: Asset What it is Cost BP_MirrorTileLive (with two Tiled mirrors) Breakable tiles showing a live reflection on both faces Medium BP_MirrorTile / BP_MirrorTile_NoSnow Breakable tiles with a still reflection Very low M_MirrorEnvironment, M_MirrorDarkCenter Shiny materials with a baked image of the room Very low BP_MirrorKitSettings One place to set every mirror's performance settings - BP_MirrorKitBudget A shared limit on mirror renders per frame -

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
A live mirror costs one scene render each time it updates, so frame time follows renders per frame, not the number of mirrors. MirrorKit keeps that down by default: mirrors you cannot see do not render, mirrors beyond 25 m keep their last image, updates are spread across frames, reflections are sized to the screen, and an optional budget caps renders per frame. A partner tunnel adds one inner render per mirror, at half rate. On Mirror Maze, partners cost about 7 % FPS.

For mirror-heavy maps, read designing maps for mirror performance: baked lighting, fewer and longer mirrors, update schedules and measured results.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Reflections of mirrors inside other independent mirrors are plausible but not geometrically exact; partners make them exact.
  • Funhouse mirrors without partners show other funhouse mirrors as dark, and InfiniteTail does not extend funhouse tunnels.
  • Sheathed weapons in first-person reflections hang on the third-person body, so they can sit slightly off the reflected body.
  • Live tiles show one reflection level; still tiles never show players.
  • Everyone on a server should use the same MirrorKit version.

Version history.

docs.title: MirrorKit version history
docs.text:
Versions are x.y.z. 1.0.0 is the full public release. Before it, only 0.y.0 versions were released on GitHub; 0.y.z with z above 0 were development builds that shipped together in the next 0.y.0 release.

Version Changes 1.0.0 Full public release: the same mirrors as 0.10.0, now in the Unchained mod registry. Licensed under GPL-3.0 from this version (0.10.0 and earlier stay MIT). 0.10.0 Style and body release (development builds 0.9.1-0.9.2):• Two choices replace six switches: Style (True / Floor / Funhouse) and Body (Full body / Head only / Stretch head / Headless / Ghost). The presets use them.• BP_Mirror_StretchHead renders at Resolution 1 with its own settings, since the effect needs detail.• Maps made with older versions: the old switches (PortalMode, MatchViewFov, ClipBehind, ScreenLevel1, HeadSource, HideBody) are now ignored, so set Style and Body on mirrors that used them without a preset. Preset mirrors and default mirrors need nothing. Add the new enums E_MirrorStyle and E_MirrorBody to the nativization exclusions if you nativize.• Efficiency: the view's field of view is measured once per frame for all mirrors instead of in every reflection render.• README rewritten around styles, bodies, partners and performance.• Network: everyone on a server should use 0.10.0. 0.9.2 Development build: efficiency: the view's field of view is measured once per frame for all mirrors instead of in every reflection render. No visible change. README rewritten around styles, bodies, partners and performance. 0.9.1 Development build: two choices replace six switches. Style (True / Floor / Funhouse) replaces PortalMode, MatchViewFov, ClipBehind and ScreenLevel1; Body (Full body / Head only / Stretch head / Headless / Ghost) replaces HeadSource and HideBody. The presets use them; BP_Mirror_StretchHead renders at Resolution 1 with its own settings. Maps made with older versions: the old switches are now ignored, so set Style and Body on mirrors that used them (funhouse, floor, headless, stretch-head or ghost mirrors placed without the presets). Preset mirrors and default mirrors need nothing. New enums E_MirrorStyle and E_MirrorBody (add them to the nativization exclusions if you nativize). 0.9.0 Partner and performance release (development builds 0.8.1-0.8.9):• Partners as a setting: facing mirror pairs render two exact levels (their own reflection and the partner's inside it); Depth is gone. Partners (on by default; no effect without a Partner) in the map settings, profiles and mirrors; servers and players switch it with ?MirrorPartners= / -MirrorPartners=, a server can forbid it with ?MirrorNoPartners. New Omega preset = Ultra plus partners; every other preset turns partners off. InfiniteTail continues a tunnel past the second level.• Pair checks: a mirror whose Partner does not point back, or that gets Partners differently, shows a red box in the editor and logs a warning; in play the pair falls back to two independent mirrors.• Reflection size follows the screen: each reflection is sized to the part of the screen it covers, never above Resolution or what the game renders (screen x resolution scale). Small and distant mirrors cost less; large partner walls get a sharper inner reflection.• Smoother partners: only the reflection levels you can see are rendered, and the inner reflection renders at half rate on a frame of its own. Measured on Mirror Maze: partners now cost about 7 % FPS (was about 6 % on the average and 12 % on the 1 % lows in 0.8.1, on a slower base).• FocusExemptFromBudget (on): off lets the capture budget slow nearby mirrors too (?MirrorFocusExempt=0).• Maps built for 0.8.0 or earlier: partnered mirrors now render as a two-level tunnel by default (set Partners off on them to keep the old single reflection), Depth 3+ shows two levels, and a mirror with a Partner needs 5 cm clear behind its face (was Depth + 3 cm, 4 cm at Depth 1).• Network: hosts on 0.9.0 send new options (MirrorPartners, MirrorNoPartners, MirrorFocusExempt) that 0.8.0 clients ignore. Everyone on a server should use 0.9.0. 0.8.9 Development build: new FocusExemptFromBudget switch (on by default, as before): off lets the capture budget slow focused (nearby / central) mirrors too. Mirror, profile and map settings; ?MirrorFocusExempt= / -MirrorFocusExempt=; presets keep the map's choice. 0.8.8 Development build: efficiency clean-up: reflection sizes are re-checked at most 10 times a second (at once after a partner change), so a reflection may stay slightly soft for up to 0.1 s when it suddenly needs more detail; the screen size and resolution scale are read once per frame for all mirrors instead of by each mirror; per-level loops replaced by direct steps. 0.8.7 Development build: a partnered mirror renders its inner reflection at half its update rate and on a frame of its own, preferably on a frame where neither it nor its partner rendered yet (if none comes before its next update, it renders with that update), so a pair you look at mostly costs one render per frame instead of two. Front reflections keep their full rate. 0.8.6 Development build: reflection sizes are capped at the size the game actually renders (r.ScreenPercentage, the in-game resolution scale), not just the screen: at 50 % a full-screen mirror stops at half the screen. DLSS keeps the screen-size cap. Mirrors whose partner pair is not live free their unused inner-reflection memory. 0.8.5 Development build: pair checks: a mirror whose Partner does not point back, or that gets Partners differently from it, shows a red box in the editor and logs a warning; in play the pair falls back to two independent mirrors instead of showing dark glass. Screen-coverage sizing: each reflection's render target follows how much of the screen it covers (level 1: the mirror on screen; level 2: the mirror as seen inside its partner), capped by the screen and by Resolution, in steps of about ×1.4 (grows at once, shrinks after 1 s). Large partner walls get a sharper inner reflection; small and distant mirrors use less memory. 0.8.4 Development build: Depth removed (more than two levels looked the same); a partnered mirror renders two levels, the second at half size. New Partners setting (on; no effect without a Partner) in the map settings, profiles and mirrors, switchable by servers and players (?MirrorPartners= / -MirrorPartners=, cap ?MirrorNoPartners). New Omega preset = Ultra plus partners; every other preset turns partners off. PerLevelResolutionMultiplier removed. Partnered mirrors need 5 cm behind the face, others 4 cm. 0.8.3 Development build: one setting, PerLevelResolutionMultiplier (default 0.5), sets how much sharper level 1 is than deeper levels: level N renders at the multiplier to the power N-1 of level 1, never below 1/8. It replaces ResolutionProfile, DeepResolutionScale, ResolutionDropPerLevel and MinimumDepthResolutionScale. Depth 2 looks the same as before; level 3 and deeper are now smaller (level 3: a quarter instead of a half). 0.8.2 Development build: partnered mirrors render only the reflection levels you can actually see (looking at one mirror of a pair needs only its odd levels and the partner's even levels), so a pair seen from one side costs about half. Partner panels are hidden once instead of before every capture. 0.8.1 Development build: InfiniteTail setting (map settings, profile or mirror; off by default). Partnered tunnels continue past Depth with the partner's own current reflection instead of ending dark. 0.8.0 First-person reflection release (development builds 0.7.1-0.7.6):• Sheathed weapons show in first-person reflections. The game hides your sheathed items from every camera in first person; MirrorKit now shows your own sheathed weapons, shields and other gear to mirrors only (never in your own view).• Put-away items: a weapon or shield you put away in first person (including to fists) appears on its sheath in reflections shortly after the swap settles, instead of only after a view switch.• On the reflected body: sheathed items follow the reflected body's pose, so a switched-off shield sits on the reflected arm.• Lighter player reflections: hair, beard and helmet follow the reflected body's pose instead of being posed separately, and dye colours are copied once a second (at once when a part changes): about a third of the per-frame work for the reflected player.• Maps need no rebuild; no network changes (players on 0.7.0 and 0.8.0 can share a server). 0.7.0 Security, memory and quality-limit release (development builds 0.6.1-0.6.6):• Server options stay private: the server shares only recognized Mirror quality settings with players; every other map option is dropped before it is sent.• Safe server presets: players only ever load the five built-in presets because of a server. A host can still use a custom preset: the host loads it and sends only the resulting values, so players do not need its PAK.• Separate rate caps: ?MirrorMaxUpdateRate= and ?MirrorMaxFocusRate= next to ?MirrorMaxRate= (both).• Off frees video memory: mirrors that start Off never reserve their reflection images, and mirrors switched Off later (a server Off reaching a joining player) release them. Switching back on creates them again.• Resolution capped at 2.0 (2560 × 1440) wherever it is set; higher values act as 2.0.• Everyone on a server needs 0.7.0: older versions do not understand every setting a 0.7.0 host sends. 0.6.0 Settings, budget, quality and smoothness release:• Settings for many mirrors: map-wide BP_MirrorKitSettings, reusable BP_MirrorProfile data assets (MP_MirrorMaze, MP_HighDetail), per-mirror SettingsSource; details-panel categories and tooltips.• New defaults = the schedule measured on MirrorMaze: Resolution 0.5, TargetUpdateRate 90 updates/s, FocusUpdateRate 144 for near/central mirrors, StaggerMode Distance, DisableReflectionAO on, ChecksEveryNFrames 4. Mirrors that kept the old defaults switch to these.• Capture budget on its own map actor BP_MirrorKitBudget (off without one): adaptive multiplier, MinUpdateRate, focus distance/angle; per-mirror ExcludeFromBudget.• MirrorQuality for players and servers: presets MQ_Off/Low/Medium/High/Ultra (all values written out), -MirrorQuality= and single values on the command line, server values and an opt-in server cap in the map options, shared with clients through BP_MirrorKitNet. MQ_Off shows plain dark glass and is reversible.• Smoothness at high FPS: SmoothUpdateInterval (on) steadies the update interval when FPS fluctuates; optional AnchorUpdateCadence; time-based rates round instead of floor; better stagger spread on grid-aligned maps.• Faster: one hidden BP_MirrorKitManager per machine runs the FPS smoothing, budget and quality parsing; mirrors cache the camera, their transform and their interval (these changes alone: +3-7 % FPS on a 268-mirror map).• Removed: the generated back face (TwoSided, TwinGap, BackPartner, BP_Mirror_TwoSided; place a second mirror behind instead, BP_MirrorTileLive gained BackWall), the off-screen test (OffscreenUpdateEveryNFrames; it cost more than it saved on large maps), the distance throttle and TelemetryMark. Maps that set them still load; the values are ignored.• Step-by-step comment boxes inside every kit Blueprint. 0.5.0 Performance and usability release (developed as internal builds after 0.4.0):• Independent mirrors: no pairing needed; one capture per face.• Cheaper per-frame work: checks before hidden-list maintenance, cached stand-ins, shared Blueprint functions, bounded loops (behaviour verified identical) and editor comment blocks.• Distances measured to the nearest point of the mirror face, centre-first and only when a feature uses them.• Exact update-slot formula (FrameCounter + phase) % N.• New settings OffscreenUpdateEveryNFrames and DisableReflectionAO; two-sided back faces inherit them.• CaptureCount / TelemetryMark diagnostics.• README rewritten; map-design guide docs/MAP-OPTIMIZATION.md. 0.4.0 Front/back partner targeting for two-sided mirrors; spacing safeguards (Depth 1-10, TwinGap minimum, clearance guide); default depth 1 0.3.0 First public release

Release notes and downloads: GitHub releases.

docs.title: Making a map with MirrorKit
docs.text: Everything a map maker needs: installing the kit in ArgonSDK, placing mirrors, settings for many mirrors at once, the capture budget, breakable tiles and every mirror setting. Players and server hosts only need the quality options. For mirror-heavy maps, also read designing maps for mirror performance.

docs.title: The mirrors
docs.text:
All live mirrors are BP_CaptureMirror or one of its presets. Presets differ only in their settings, and every setting can be changed on any placed mirror.

Asset What you see Cost BP_CaptureMirror True reflection: your full body (moving legs, head, weapon in hand), other players and the room. With a facing Partner, an infinite-looking tunnel High BP_Mirror_Funhouse Magnified, gappy carnival look (Style Funhouse) High BP_Mirror_Headless Your reflection has no head; others look normal (Body Headless) High BP_Mirror_StretchHead Your head stretches as you look up and down (Body Stretch head; its own settings at Resolution 1, since the effect needs detail) High BP_Mirror_Ghost Your body is invisible; your weapons float (Body Ghost) High BP_MirrorTileLive + two Tiled mirrors A wall of breakable tiles showing a live reflection on both faces; break one and walk through Medium (one reflection level) BP_MirrorTile / BP_MirrorTile_NoSnow Breakable tiles with a baked (still) reflection; the snow variant plays wind when broken Very low M_MirrorEnvironment Material: shiny metal with a baked image of the room, plus screen-space reflections at shallow angles Very low M_MirrorDarkCenter Material: reflects at shallow angles, black when looking straight at it Very low

Every effect is per viewer. A ghost or headless mirror changes only your own reflection as you see it; other players see you normally in their mirrors.

docs.title: Install the kit in ArgonSDK
docs.text:
1. Unzip MirrorKit_Source.zip.
  2. Copy its Content folder's contents to ArgonSDK/Content/Mods/MirrorKit/, so you get ArgonSDK/Content/Mods/MirrorKit/Blueprints/BP_CaptureMirror.uasset. This location matters. Unreal names assets by folder (/Game/Mods/MirrorKit/...), and MirrorKit.pak loads them under the same names in game. Do not move or rename kit assets; your map would then point at assets the shared PAK does not contain. A folder link is fine.
  3. Copy MirrorKit.pak into your game's TBL/Content/Paks/ to test.

docs.title: Place a live mirror
docs.text:
1. Drag BP_CaptureMirror (or a preset) into the level.
  2. The mirror's local +X axis points out of its reflective face, and the face is at the actor's origin.
  3. Switch the transform gizmo to Local to see it.
  4. Turn wall mirrors with Rotation Z (Yaw).
  5. Size it with the actor scale: Y × 100 = width in cm, Z × 100 = height in cm, and keep X = 1. For example, (1, 12, 6) is a 12 × 6 m mirror. For a floor mirror, rotate it to face up.
  6. Leave Partner empty for a normal mirror (see Partners for the tunnel effect).
  7. Leave 4 cm clear behind the face (5 cm when the mirror has a Partner). The reflection layers live there; geometry inside that space flickers. Selecting a mirror shows an orange ClearanceGuide box over this space; it has no collision and is hidden in game.
  8. Mirrors are solid: the backing plate blocks players and weapons, except in Tiled mirrors, where the tiles collide. The back of a mirror shows plain metal. For a mirror wall that reflects on both sides, place a second mirror on the back facing the other way (see spacing below).
  9. Nothing else to place. The stand-ins that draw your body in reflections (BP_MirrorDouble*) spawn automatically.

Spacing rules (MirrorKit cannot move your geometry, so these are up to you):

Behind a mirror face Keep at least (without / with a Partner) Walls, floors, any map geometry 4 / 5 cm (the orange box) Another mirror back to back (no wall between) 5 / 6 cm between the two faces (the larger if only one has a partner) A wall between two back-to-back mirrors 4 / 5 cm on each side of the wall (36 cm wall: faces 44 / 46 cm apart)

Giving a mirror a Partner later means re-checking these gaps: a partnered mirror needs 1 cm more behind the face.

docs.title: Build your map so it works with the shared PAK
docs.text:
• Use your own meshes and materials for structure. Place only kit actors and kit mirror materials. A player without MirrorKit then still gets a playable map instead of holes in it.
  • Your PAK must not contain MirrorKit's files. Cooking your map also writes cooked kit files to Saved/Cooked/.../Content/Mods/MirrorKit/; package only your own mod folder.
  • Keep the kit's enums out of native conversion. If your project uses Blueprint nativization:
  • Add /Game/Mods/MirrorKit/Blueprints/E_MirrorStaggerMode, /Game/Mods/MirrorKit/Blueprints/E_MirrorSettingsSource, /Game/Mods/MirrorKit/Blueprints/E_MirrorStyle and /Game/Mods/MirrorKit/Blueprints/E_MirrorBody as +ExcludedAssets under [BlueprintNativizationSettings] in Config/DefaultEditor.ini.
  • Otherwise UE 4.25 can leave them out of the PAK.
  • Recook referring maps after changing this.
  • Add MirrorKit as a dependency in your mod.json.

docs.title: Settings for many mirrors at once
docs.text:
Every mirror works with no extra setup: its defaults are the schedule tuned on MirrorMaze (half resolution, 90 updates per second). The mirror, BP_MirrorKitSettings and new profiles start from the same values, so placing a settings actor changes nothing until you edit it. The capture budget is the exception: it is off unless the map has a BP_MirrorKitBudget, and placing one turns it on (budget 2 captures per frame by default).

Two optional map actors, both in Blueprints/ (drag each in at most once; they have no mesh or collision and players never see them):

Actor Sets Applies to BP_MirrorKitSettings the per-mirror performance settings below mirrors with SettingsSource MapDefault (and Profile mirrors without a profile) BP_MirrorKitBudget the budget: CaptureBudget, CaptureBudgetMaxMultiplier, MinUpdateRate, BudgetFocusDistance, BudgetFocusAngle every mirror, whatever its SettingsSource (the budget is shared by the whole map)

Each mirror picks where its per-mirror settings come from with SettingsSource (category MirrorKit › Settings):

SettingsSource The mirror uses MapDefault (default) the map's BP_MirrorKitSettings; its own values if the map has none Profile the MirrorProfile data asset in its Profile slot; with no profile assigned, the map's settings actor Own its own values
  • Whole map: edit BP_MirrorKitSettings (or leave it out and keep the defaults).
  • Groups: right-click in the Content Browser › Miscellaneous › Data Asset › BP_MirrorProfile to make a profile. Set SettingsSource to Profile on the group and pick it; editing the profile changes the whole group. Shipped: Profiles/MP_MirrorMaze (the MirrorMaze schedule, so a group keeps it if you change the map settings) and Profiles/MP_HighDetail (full resolution at 120 updates/s).
  • One-offs: set SettingsSource to Own and edit that mirror.
  • Budget: edit BP_MirrorKitBudget; mirrors, profiles and settings actors never carry it. At runtime a hidden BP_MirrorKitManager (spawned automatically, nothing to place) applies it. Without a budget actor the budget is off. Placing one turns it on with its defaults (budget 2, max ×4, min 30 updates/s, focus 800 cm / 15°), visible and editable on the actor. To keep one mirror out of it (e.g. a showcase mirror), tick its ExcludeFromBudget.

Per-mirror performance settings: Resolution, UpdateEveryNFrames, TargetUpdateRate, FocusUpdateRate, StaggerMode, DistanceStaggerStart, CaptureDistance, MaxViewDistance, VisibilityTolerance, ChecksEveryNFrames, DisableReflectionAO, SmoothUpdateInterval, AnchorUpdateCadence, FocusExemptFromBudget, plus the look settings InfiniteTail and Partners. Body, Partner and tile settings stay on each mirror; a MapDefault mirror takes all of the above from BP_MirrorKitSettings, so set Partners there (or use a profile) rather than on single mirrors. Settings are resolved when the match starts; player and server quality choices are applied on top (again if the server options arrive later).

For a single sharp, every-frame mirror (the defaults before 0.6.0), set SettingsSource Own, Resolution 1, TargetUpdateRate 0, UpdateEveryNFrames 1, StaggerMode None, DisableReflectionAO off, and ExcludeFromBudget on.

docs.title: How the settings pieces fit
docs.text:
Piece Who makes it Job BP_MirrorKitSettings map maker (placed, one per map) default look and schedule for every MapDefault mirror BP_MirrorProfile map maker (data asset) the same settings for a group of mirrors (SettingsSource = Profile) BP_MirrorKitBudget map maker (placed, optional) budget rules; without it the budget is off BP_MirrorQuality (MQ_*) kit / anyone (data assets) MirrorQuality presets for players and servers BP_MirrorKitManager spawned automatically by the first mirror, every machine reads the budget actor and the quality options once, smooths the FPS and runs the budget each frame BP_MirrorKitNet spawned automatically on a server whose map options include mirror options carries the server options to clients

Each mirror: own values, then BP_MirrorKitSettings or its profile (ResolveSettings), then the manager's quality layers and budget rules; afterwards it only re-reads when the manager reports a change.

docs.title: Mirror settings
docs.text:
All settings are on every placed mirror. The performance defaults are the MirrorMaze schedule (see above for the sharp, every-frame values used before 0.6.0). With SettingsSource MapDefault or Profile, the per-mirror performance settings come from the settings actor or profile when there is one; the budget is not a mirror setting (see the budget table below).

Look and body

Setting Default What it does Style True True: a true reflection. Floor: for large floor mirrors seen from above, sharper looking straight down (keep nothing below the mirror). Funhouse: magnified carnival look with gaps at the edges. Floor and Funhouse render their front reflection at full screen size (the most expensive kind) Body Full body Your body in this mirror: Full body, Head only (head and torso, stiff head), Stretch head (head stretches as you look up and down), Headless, or Ghost (invisible body, weapons float). Other players always look normal FitVisible on Render only the part of the mirror inside your view (sharper close up; Style True and Floor) Tiled off The mirror is invisible and walk-through; tiles show its reflection

Partners

Setting Default What it does Partner none Facing mirror for the tunnel effect; empty = independent mirror. Needs 5 cm clear behind the face (spacing rules) Partners on A mirror with a Partner renders the geometric tunnel: two levels, its own reflection and the partner's reflection inside it (each mirror of a working pair renders one extra inner reflection, at half its update rate and sized to the screen). No effect without a Partner. Off = the pair renders like independent mirrors. Map settings, profile or mirror; servers and players can switch it (quality options). Both mirrors of a pair must point at each other and get Partners the same way (same SettingsSource; same Profile, or the same value when Own). MapDefault mirrors on a map without BP_MirrorKitSettings use their own values, so they also need the same value. The red box updates when a mirror is edited (not when a settings actor is added or removed, or a sublevel loads later), so treat it as a hint and re-select the pair after such changes. Otherwise a red box shows over the mirror in the editor, a warning is logged, and in play the pair renders as two independent mirrors

Resolution

Setting Default What it does Resolution 0.5 The largest render target a reflection may use: 1 = 1280 × 720, the default 0.5 = 640 × 360. Each reflection is sized to how much of your screen it covers (about one target pixel per screen pixel), never above this and never above the size the game renders (screen size x the in-game resolution scale), so small or distant mirrors cost less and large partner walls get their inner reflection at up to the full size. Sizes step by about ×1.4, grow at once and shrink after a second. Maximum 2.0 (2560 × 1440); higher values, from any source, act as 2.0

Performance

Setting Default What it does UpdateEveryNFrames 2 Update every N frames (used when TargetUpdateRate is 0); skipped frames reuse the last reflection. 2 roughly halves capture work StaggerMode Distance Spread updates across frames: Distributed (all mirrors) or Distance (mirrors at or beyond DistanceStaggerStart). Needed with N > 1 to keep worst-case frames smooth DistanceStaggerStart 1000 cm Face distance where Distance staggering begins CaptureDistance 2500 cm Stop updating beyond this face distance (the mirror keeps its last image) MaxViewDistance 0 Limit how far each capture renders into the reflected scene; 0 = unlimited VisibilityTolerance 0.2 s Stop updating when neither this mirror nor its partner has been drawn for this long DisableReflectionAO on Skip ambient occlusion inside this mirror's reflections (cheaper, rarely visible) TargetUpdateRate 90 (0 = off) Target reflection updates per second; when set, replaces UpdateEveryNFrames with round(FPS ÷ rate) frames, at least 1 (e.g. 90: every 3 frames at 300 FPS, every frame at 60). Below about 1.5 × the rate (135 FPS for 90/s) every update is every frame FocusUpdateRate 144 (0 = off) Updates per second for focused mirrors: face within 800 cm or centre within 15° of your view (the budget actor's BudgetFocusDistance/BudgetFocusAngle when one is placed). Keeps close reflections smooth at high uncapped FPS, where 90/s holds each reflection for several frames. Costs nothing below about 135 FPS (90/s is already every frame there); 1000 = every frame. Players can change it with MirrorQuality (-MirrorFocusRate=); a server cap can limit it ChecksEveryNFrames 4 Run the expensive per-mirror checks (distance, focus) only on the mirror's due frames and otherwise every N frames; 1 = every frame SmoothUpdateInterval on Base the update interval on the FPS averaged over ~0.5 s and keep it until the FPS clearly moves, so it does not flip with frame-time noise. Removes most jitter at fluctuating or uncapped FPS (measured: about 0-3 % FPS uncapped, none at a 240 cap) AnchorUpdateCadence off Optional: count each interval from the mirror's last update, so a changed interval never produces one short or long gap (off = fixed slots (FrameCounter + phase) % N). No visible gain over smoothing alone in our tests and about 2-5 % FPS uncapped, so it is off by default; worth trying on PCs where smoothing alone still judders InfiniteTail off Partnered mirrors: past the second (last exact) level, show the partner's own current reflection instead of dark glass, so the tunnel keeps going (approximate, no extra renders) FocusExemptFromBudget on Mirrors near you or near the centre of your view (the budget's focus distance and angle) keep their pace while the capture budget slows the others. Off: the budget slows them too, which smooths the worst frames when many mirrors are close at once, at the cost of nearby reflections updating less often under load. Servers and players can switch it (MirrorFocusExempt) ExcludeFromBudget off Keep this mirror out of the map-wide budget: never counted and never slowed down by it

Budget (map-wide, on BP_MirrorKitBudget; off without one; defaults below are the actor's)

Setting Default What it does CaptureBudget 2 (0 = off) Target captures per frame across all mirrors; when the smoothed load is over it, every mirror's interval is stretched (mirrors with ExcludeFromBudget are left out) CaptureBudgetMaxMultiplier 4 Largest interval stretch the budget may apply MinUpdateRate 30 (0 = off) The capture budget never stretches a mirror below this many updates per second BudgetFocusDistance 800 cm While the budget is stretching intervals, mirrors whose face is this close keep their normal interval (0 = off) BudgetFocusAngle 15° While the budget is stretching intervals, mirrors whose centre is within this angle of your view direction (0 = off)

"Face distance" means the camera's distance to the nearest point of the mirror, not to its centre.

docs.title: How a mirror decides to update
docs.text:
Each frame, a mirror goes through three steps:

  1. Schedule. Every tick increments FrameCounter. An update is due when (FrameCounter + phase) % N == 0; with AnchorUpdateCadence (optional), after the first update it is due when N frames have passed since the last one.
  2. N is round(FPS ÷ TargetUpdateRate) (at least 1; with SmoothUpdateInterval the FPS is averaged over ~0.5 s and N changes only when the ratio is 0.65 or more away from it), or UpdateEveryNFrames when the rate is 0. Focused mirrors use FocusUpdateRate instead when that gives a shorter interval. Unfocused mirrors are then multiplied by the capture-budget multiplier (1 when CaptureBudget is off), never below MinUpdateRate.
  3. phase is 0 unless the mirror is staggered (or the budget multiplier is above 1); then it is floor(PhaseHash × N). PhaseHash is computed once at start-up from the mirror's position (Fraction(Sin(0.0129898X + 0.078233Y + 0.037719Z) × 43758.5453)), which spreads grid-aligned mirrors evenly.
  4. Capture budget (CaptureBudget > 0): mirrors report their captures to the hidden BP_MirrorKitManager. Once a frame it smooths the total, and at most every 0.2 s steps a shared multiplier up (load over budget) or down (the load at one step lower would fit the budget), from 1 to CaptureBudgetMaxMultiplier. While the multiplier is above 1, focused mirrors (face within BudgetFocusDistance, or centre inside the BudgetFocusAngle view cone) keep their unstretched interval, so the mirrors you look at stay smooth.
  5. Eligibility. All of these must hold:
  6. you have a local camera;
  7. the face distance is under CaptureDistance;
  8. you are in front of the face;
  9. the mirror (or its partner) was drawn within VisibilityTolerance.

"Drawn" includes being seen inside another mirror. Distances check the centre distance first and compute the exact nearest point only when needed. 3. Capture. Level 1 is rendered (fitted to the visible part with FitVisible), then deeper partner levels.

Independent mirrors show other mirrors' images inside their reflection. Those images were rendered for your own viewpoint, so mirror-in-mirror repetitions are plausible but not geometrically exact. Partners give exact nested reflections, at the cost of one render per level.

DisableReflectionAO works through a stored post-process override (AO intensity 0) whose blend weight the checkbox raises at start-up.

A mirror's size, settings, position and facing are read when play starts (the camera is read once per tick). Do not resize live mirrors at runtime; after moving or turning one at runtime, call its RefreshMirrorTransform.

docs.title: Partners and tunnels
docs.text:
• Set two facing mirrors as each other's Partner for a tunnel: each shows its own reflection and the partner's reflection inside it (two exact levels; more looked no different in our tests). Set relationships before play starts.
  • With InfiniteTail on, the tunnel continues past the second level with approximate reflections instead of ending dark.
  • Partners (on by default) switches the tunnel; Each mirror of a working pair renders one extra inner reflection, at half its update rate and sized to the screen. The built-in quality presets other than Omega switch partners off, so on a server or for a player who picks Low to Ultra the pair renders like independent mirrors. Leave it on in your map settings if the tunnel is the point of the map, or off if the map should be cheap by default and the tunnel opt-in (Omega, ?MirrorPartners=1).
  • Partners do not have to be parallel: each reflection is computed across each mirror's own plane.
  • A mirror on the back of a wall is an ordinary mirror, so it takes its own Partner.
  • Partners are mutual pairs. Each mirror of a pair names the other as its Partner. Chains or one-sided links (A → B → C → A) are not supported: those mirrors render as independent mirrors, and the editor shows the red box.

docs.title: Tiles and materials
docs.text:
Breakable live tiles

  1. Place a BP_CaptureMirror covering the wall's front, and a second one back to back covering its back (facing the other way, spaced as in the spacing rules). Turn on Tiled on both and leave Partner empty.
  2. Place BP_MirrorTileLive tiles across them, centred between the two faces, with thickness about the gap. For example, scale (1.5, 0.06, 2.0) is a 150 × 200 cm tile for a 6 cm gap.
  3. Set each tile's Wall to the front mirror and BackWall to the back mirror. A tile without BackWall shows plain metal on its back.

A broken tile disappears on both faces and leaves a walk-through hole, with one health bar per tile.

Baked tiles. Place BP_MirrorTile (snow wind on break) or BP_MirrorTile_NoSnow and scale to the tile size. They use SM_MirrorTile and SM_MirrorTile_Cracked by default, and never show players. To match your room's shine, use your own environment material instance on their StaticMesh.

Environment material. M_MirrorEnvironment shows a baked 360° image (cubemap) where screen-space reflections have nothing. To match your room:

  1. Place a Scene Capture Cube at the surface, at head height.
  2. Assign a Cube Render Target and capture.
  3. Right-click the render target and choose Create Static Texture.
  4. Create a Material Instance of M_MirrorEnvironment in your map's folder and set Environment (plus EnvStrength, Tint and Roughness if wanted).
  5. Apply it, then delete the capture actor.

docs.title: Online play
docs.text: Each player's game renders mirrors from their own camera, so everyone sees a correct reflection. Your stand-in exists only on your machine; other players see your real body. Breakable tiles use the game's own breakable windows: the server decides when a tile breaks, and everyone sees it. Dedicated servers do no mirror rendering and spawn no stand-ins.

docs.title: Reading the Blueprints
docs.text:
Open BP_CaptureMirror. EventGraph resolves the settings, finds the manager and applies its quality, then routes to InitializeMirror; Tick goes to UpdateMirror; double-click the calls to follow the work. Each function's tooltip says what it does; inside larger functions, comment boxes mark each step (what that group of nodes does). BP_MirrorKitManager, the tile and the stand-in Blueprints follow the same style. Functions are grouped by category:

Category Functions Lifecycle InitializeMirror, UpdateMirror, SyncWithManager Setup ResolveSettings (first at BeginPlay), SnapshotQualityBase, EnsureManager, ApplyManagerQuality, ReadManagerBudget, ApplyQualityValues, ApplyQualityCaps, ApplyMirrorsOff, RefreshMirrorTransform, ConfigureBacking, ConfigureTileMode, InitializeCaptureResources, InitializeFirstCapture, InitializeDeepCapture, EnsurePlayerStandIn Scheduling ResolvePartner, UpdateCaptureBudget, AdvanceCaptureSchedule, CheckCaptureEligibility, IsWithinFaceDistance, DistanceToMirrorFace Capture CaptureReflectionStack, CapturePortalFirst, CapturePortalDeep, CaptureLegacyView Projection ReflectViewAcrossPlane, ProjectMirrorRay, FitMirrorInterval, ComputeVisibleMirrorBounds (pure maths) Visibility RefreshCaptureHiddenActors, HideActorFromActiveCaptures, HidePartnerPanelsForCapture

BP_MirrorKitManager: FilterServerOptions (resolves presets on the host and serializes only numeric settings and flags), ApplyServerOptions (parses the quality layers), ResolveBudget (reads BP_MirrorKitBudget), and a Tick that smooths the FPS and steps the budget multiplier.

Capture count. Each mirror counts its captures in CaptureCount. The capture budget uses it: each tick a budgeted mirror reports its captures since the last report to BP_MirrorKitManager.

docs.title: Designing maps for mirror performance
docs.text: Chivalry 2 is competitive, and many players run 144-240+ FPS. Every live mirror renders the scene again, so a mirror-heavy map can lose a lot of frame rate. This guide covers what a map designer can do about it. The advice is based on measurements on MirrorMaze, listed at the end.

docs.title: The one rule: count captures, not mirrors
docs.text:
Each time a live mirror updates, it renders the scene once. That is a capture. Frame time grows with the number of captures per frame. Mirror size and render-target resolution matter much less.

  • Measured: roughly 0.2-0.3 ms per capture on the test PC (Resolution 0.35-0.5). FPS followed captures-per-frame second by second.
  • Lowering resolution from 0.5 to 0.35 saved only about 0.14 ms per frame once captures were reduced.

Everything below reduces captures, makes each capture cheaper, or spreads captures evenly across frames.

docs.title: 1. Bake your lighting (biggest single gain)
docs.text:
Movable lights are recalculated in every view, so each mirror capture redoes the lighting. With static (baked) lights, walls and floors read precomputed light maps, which is cheap in the main view and in every capture.

  • Measured: +23% walking, +31% standing (243 → 298 and 239 → 313 FPS on the test PC). Captures per frame stayed the same; each one just got cheaper.
  • How:
  • Set lights to Static.
  • In World Settings, turn off Force No Precomputed Lighting.
  • Make sure meshes have a lightmap UV channel.
  • Build lighting.
  • Set decoration meshes without lightmap UVs (unlit trims, decals, floor guides) to Movable.
  • Shadows on static lights are free at runtime. Turning them on gives real dark corners and contact shadows.
  • Large single meshes (a whole floor or ceiling) get coarse light maps that show as soft squares and grain. Some find this adds character; split the mesh into tiles if you want it smooth.
  • Trade-offs: lights cannot change in game. Players are lit from stored light samples rather than direct light, so they look slightly flatter.
  • General baking pitfall, not mirror-specific: overlapping faces in the same plane (for example a wall running into a pillar of equal width) flicker once baked.
  • Do not try to switch lights off only inside mirrors. Chivalry 2 is a shipping build, and the engine ignores light-type show flags there.

docs.title: 2. Use fewer, longer mirrors
docs.text:
A wall built from several mirror pieces captures once per piece. One mirror covering the same flat run captures once.

  • Measured on a 463-piece maze:
Merge Mirrors Walking FPS Standing FPS None 463 223 220 Touching pieces merged 326 246 231 Also merged across pillar and junction gaps 243 252 258

Merging across pillar gaps cut captures per frame by 25-35%. - Pieces must lie in the same plane, face the same way and share their settings. - A mirror may run behind a pillar: the pillar hides that part, and reflections still show the pillar. - Do not run a mirror behind the end of a wall that meets the mirror face. The wall end sits inside the mirror's render-panel layer (the first few centimetres behind the face) and flickers, which is most visible with baked shadows. Split the mirror at such junctions instead. - Very long mirrors spread one render target over more wall, so they look slightly softer. Resolution 0.5 compensates cheaply.

docs.title: 3. Update every other frame, staggered
docs.text:
• UpdateEveryNFrames = 2 halves capture work. Measured: about −2.5 to −3.3 ms per frame (136 → 208 FPS walking at the time). Fast motion in reflections is slightly less smooth; testers noticed it only when looking for it.
  • On its own, every mirror updates on the same frame, so frames alternate heavy and light, and the worst frames (1% low) do not improve.
  • Add StaggerMode = Distance (or Distributed) to spread mirrors across frames. Measured: 1% low improved from about 110 to 138 FPS walking (187 standing), with the best average as well.
  • Staggering is phase-based: (FrameCounter + phase) % N == 0, with the phase taken from the mirror's position. Since 0.6.0 the phase hash spreads grid-aligned mirrors evenly (the old one clustered them on one phase).
  • Large maps can be CPU-bound on Blueprint ticks. On MirrorMaze (263 mirrors) the off-screen test cost more processor time than it saved: turning it off gave +52 FPS standing and +32 walking, so 0.6.0 removed it. Captures had become cheap (about 0.085 ms each). Keep the lean tick (ChecksEveryNFrames 4, the default).

docs.title: 3b. Recommended schedule for mirror-heavy maps
docs.text:
Since 0.6.0 these are the defaults of every mirror (plus Resolution 0.5, StaggerMode Distance and DisableReflectionAO on). Change them map-wide with BP_MirrorKitSettings (per-mirror settings) and BP_MirrorKitBudget (the budget rows below); see Settings for many mirrors at once in the map-making guide.

Use time, not frames, and let a budget trim the far mirrors:

Setting Value Why TargetUpdateRate 90 ~every 3 frames at 300 FPS, every frame at 60 FPS (frame-based every-2 is only 30 updates/s at a 60 FPS cap; testers saw it as choppy) CaptureBudget 2 captures per frame across the map; stretches far, off-centre mirrors when the load is higher BudgetFocusDistance / BudgetFocusAngle 800 cm / 15° (defaults) mirrors near you or near the view centre keep their pace while FocusExemptFromBudget is on (without focus, budgets looked choppy in bouts) MinUpdateRate 30 the budget never pushes a mirror below 30 updates/s (at a 60 FPS cap that means at most every 2nd frame) FocusUpdateRate 144 focused mirrors (near or central) update faster, against sideways jitter at high uncapped FPS (free below about 216 FPS, where 144/s is already every frame)

Measured on MirrorMaze (263 mirrors after merging): 327 FPS walking uncapped (every-2 without budget: ~291; no mirrors: ~379), 1% low ~207. At a 60 FPS cap, mirrors update 30-60 times a second at ~36 % GPU, and testers saw them as smooth. Keep TargetUpdateRate well below your usual FPS: with rounding, a mirror drops to every frame only below 1.5 × the rate.

docs.title: 3c. Smoothness at high frame rates
docs.text:
Rate-based schedules make a mirror update every round(FPS / rate) frames, so the faster the PC, the more frames each reflection is held. Below about 135 FPS the default 90 updates/s is already every frame; jitter is a high-FPS question.

Finding Measured Setting Sideways strafing next to a mirror looked jittery uncapped (~300 FPS) walking: no focus 355, focus 144/s 315, focus every frame 281 FPS; 144 greatly reduced it, every frame removed it FocusUpdateRate 144 by default; players/hosts raise it with -MirrorFocusRate=1000 / ?MirrorFocusRate=1000 The interval flipped between N and N+1 with frame-time noise near rounding boundaries, giving uneven gaps smoothed interval visibly steadier at ~0-3 % FPS uncapped, no cost at a 240 cap; an anchored cadence added no visible gain for ~2-5 % SmoothUpdateInterval on (default), AnchorUpdateCadence optional Close first-person strafing still slightly choppy at 144/s above ~216 FPS confirmed by -MirrorFocusRate=1000 (not resolution, not tick order) default kept at 144 by choice; Ultra preset = every frame

0.6.0 also made the per-mirror Blueprint work cheaper (interval stored once per tick; one hidden manager for FPS smoothing, budget and quality). On MirrorMaze, same map and settings, uncapped, these changes alone gave +7 % standing (360 -> 385 FPS), +3 % walking (320 -> 330) and better 1 % lows.

Judge smoothness on the display you play on: on a 60 Hz screen, uncapped FPS mainly lowers input latency, and a 60 (or 120/180) cap gives the cleanest picture because every mirror then updates every frame.

docs.title: 4. Settings worth knowing
docs.text:
Setting Effect measured Visual cost Recommendation Resolution 0.5 → 0.35 about +3% (8 FPS walking) after the steps above softer reflections 0.5 is a good default; drop only if GPU-bound with many mirrors DisableReflectionAO about −1 ms standing in early tests (every-frame updates); overlaps with resolution not noticeable in mirrors on by default CaptureDistance 15 m −1.75 ms walking distant mirrors visibly freeze prefer staggering and merging; keep the default 25 m unless the layout hides distant mirrors MaxViewDistance small (+6-9 FPS at 25-15 m from a ~40 FPS baseline, older kit) removes distant geometry from reflections rarely worth it in closed layouts Partners on (partnered mirrors) each mirror of a working pair renders one extra inner reflection, at half its update rate and sized to the screen tunnel effect use only where the effect is the point; off in every preset except Omega

CaptureDistance and DistanceStaggerStart measure to the nearest point of the mirror face, so long mirrors stay live near their ends.

docs.title: 5. Layout habits
docs.text:
• Corners where two mirrors face each other keep both live even when one is only visible inside the other.
  • Mirrors behind the player, or outside the view, still count while they appear in other reflections; mirrors drawn nowhere stop after VisibilityTolerance.
  • Mirrors inside the view but hidden behind walls can still capture when they appear in a reflection; the engine does not tell Blueprints about main-view occlusion. Breaking long sight lines between mirrors helps.
  • Decorative surfaces that do not need a live player reflection should use baked tiles (BP_MirrorTile) or M_MirrorEnvironment instead of live mirrors.

docs.title: 6. Partners and reflection size (kit 0.8.5-0.8.7, measured on Mirror Maze with 20 partner pairs)
docs.text:
Same route, uncapped, single runs each (identical builds differ by about 7 % on the mean):

Kit FPS mean p5 1 % low worst dip 0.8.2 (fixed-size reflections) 312 284 193 155 0.8.6 (sized to screen coverage) 330-353 265-298 218-239 111-120 0.8.7 (inner reflection on its own frame) 379 332 260 173 0.8.7 with FocusUpdateRate 90 408 368 285 205
  • Sizing reflections to screen coverage helps every mirror, partnered or not: small and distant mirrors get small targets.
  • A lower in-game resolution scale raises the average but not the dips, which are not about pixel count.
  • Partner walls you stand near are "focused" (they skip the budget and update at FocusUpdateRate, 144/s by default). That is a large share of their steady cost. 90/s cuts it further, at the risk of slight sideways judder above about 200 FPS.
  • The deepest dips came from a pair's two renders landing in one frame. Since 0.8.7, the inner reflection renders at half rate on a frame of its own; it did not look choppier in testing.
  • One-off ~1 s dips (worst moment about a third of the average FPS) remain with mirrors, partners or not; a map without mirrors has only shallower ones. Counting focused mirrors in the budget (FocusExemptFromBudget off) lifts the average 3-6 % but not these dips.
  • Known limits: a resized reflection leaves its old render target to garbage collection (freeing it at once would stall rendering), so video memory can run above the live targets until the next collection; and an inner reflection queued for its own frame can still render once after you look away (at most a few frames later).

docs.title: How these numbers were measured
docs.text:
• Map: MirrorMaze (463 mirror pieces at first, 263 after merging coplanar pieces; 81 point lights), one PC, solo, frame-rate cap off.
  • Machine: GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 (8 GB, driver 32.0.16.1074 = 610.74); CPU Intel Core i7-14700F (20 cores / 28 threads); 32 GB RAM; Windows 11 Home (build 26200). Game: 1920 × 1080 fullscreen, VSync off, sg.* quality 3 (Epic) except foliage and shading 1, resolution scale 100 %. Values read on 2026-10-17 from Windows and GameUserSettings.ini; earlier measurements are assumed to use the same machine.
  • Recording: NVIDIA App performance logs. Each case is recorded as 30 s standing at spawn plus one fixed walking route, repeated in alternating order (2-3 rounds).
  • Telemetry: captures per frame come from each mirror's CaptureCount, read by test tools. Absolute FPS differs per PC; use the relative changes.
Step (cumulative, walking) FPS Baseline, every frame, Resolution 0.5 136 AO off + Resolution 0.35 ("Lite") 144 + every 2 frames + Distance stagger 222 + merged mirrors (243) 252 Resolution back to 0.5 243 + baked static lighting 298 (no mirrors at all) 379

docs.title: Mirror quality options
docs.text: Players and server hosts can change how MirrorKit mirrors look and how much they cost, without touching the map. This page lists every option. For a quick start, see Mirror quality on the home page.

docs.title: Where the options go
docs.text:
Where Who Format Launch options in the Unchained Launcher (Settings › Advanced Settings › CLI Arguments) a player, for their own game -Key=Value, e.g. -MirrorQuality=Low The map's Options box in the main menu, or the server's map options a server host for everyone on the server; also you when playing offline (you are the server then) ?Key=Value, e.g. ?MirrorQuality=High

Several options go one after another: -MirrorQuality=Low -MirrorFocusRate=1000 or ?MirrorQuality=High?MirrorMaxRate=90. In the Options box, -Key=Value does nothing; use ?.

docs.title: How the layers combine
docs.text:
From first to last; a later layer wins:

  1. Map: the map maker's settings.
  2. Server values (optional): ?MirrorQuality= and single values in the map options. Everyone on the server starts from these instead of the map's.
  3. Your choice (optional): -MirrorQuality= and single values in your launch options. Up or down, freely.
  4. Server cap (optional): ?MirrorMaxQuality= and limits in the map options. Only values above a limit are lowered, for everyone on the server, including players who chose nothing. Without a cap you can raise as you like.

If nobody chooses anything, mirrors run the map's settings.

Example: with -MirrorQuality=Low in your launch options and ?MirrorQuality=High in the Options box when playing offline, you get Low: the Options box sets the server values, and your own launch choice comes after them. Only a cap (?MirrorMaxQuality=) can limit your choice, and a cap only lowers.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
Preset Resolution Updates per second Nearest mirrors Distance Captures per frame Reflection AO Smoothing Anchor Partners Omega 1.0 144 every frame 40 m no budget on on off on Ultra 1.0 144 every frame 40 m no budget on on off off High 0.5 90 144 25 m 2 off on off off Medium 0.5 60 60 20 m 3 off on off off Low 0.35 45 45 15 m 2 off on off off Off no live reflections; mirrors show plain dark glass

Partners are facing mirror pairs a map maker linked for a tunnel effect (a reflection inside a reflection). They cost extra (each mirror of a working pair renders one extra inner reflection, at half its update rate and sized to the screen), so only Omega turns them on. To keep a preset and add partners, follow it with the single value: ?MirrorQuality=High?MirrorPartners=1 (server) or -MirrorQuality=High -MirrorPartners=1 (your own game). Maps without partnered mirrors look the same in Omega and Ultra. To switch on only partners and keep everything else as the map sets it, use ?MirrorPartners=1 (server) or -MirrorPartners=1 (your own game).

Partners on (Mirror Maze, ?MirrorPartners=1) Partners off (Mirror Maze default) Facing mirrors show each other correctly: the reflection inside the reflection continues the corridor (the tunnel on the right). Each mirror reflects on its own; reflections of other mirrors are approximate, so the geometry inside them looks wrong.

Server map options ?MirrorQuality= and ?MirrorMaxQuality= accept built-in names or the path of a custom BP_MirrorQuality asset installed on the host. The host loads and checks the preset, applies inline settings, and sends only the resulting numeric values and flags to clients. Clients do not need the custom preset PAK. Missing or wrong-type presets contribute no values; inline settings still apply.

For example, install your preset PAK on the server and use ?MirrorQuality=/Game/Mods/MyPresets/MQ_Server. Use ?MirrorMaxQuality=/Game/Mods/MyPresets/MQ_ServerCap to apply a custom preset as limits. Use MirrorKit 0.7.0 or later on both host and clients; older clients do not understand every setting the host sends.

For your own game, use a preset name (-MirrorQuality=Low) or explicitly choose a BP_MirrorQuality asset from a PAK you installed (-MirrorQuality=/Game/Mods/<Mod>/<Asset>). This local launch option retains custom-asset loading; it is your choice and is not supplied by the server. The custom PAK is needed only on machines choosing that local preset. An unknown local preset changes nothing.

docs.title: Single values
docs.text:
The same keys work as launch options (-Key=) and as server values (?Key=). They apply after the preset in the same layer.

Key Value Changes MirrorResolution e.g. 0.5, 1; at most 2 Largest reflection size (1 = 1280 × 720, 2 = 2560 × 1440). Each reflection is sized to the part of your screen it covers and never exceeds what the game renders (your screen x the in-game resolution scale), so a high value costs only where a mirror is large on screen. Values above 2 act as 2 MirrorRate updates per second, e.g. 90; 0 = every N frames How often mirrors update MirrorFocusRate updates per second; 1000 = every frame How often the nearest and most central mirrors update MirrorDistance cm, e.g. 2500 Mirrors farther than this stop updating MirrorCaptures captures per frame; 0 = budget off The capture budget MirrorAO 0 off, 1 on Ambient occlusion inside reflections MirrorSmooth 0 off, 1 on Steady update interval when FPS fluctuates MirrorAnchor 0 off, 1 on Count each interval from the last update MirrorPartners 0 off, 1 on Partnered mirror tunnels (a reflection inside a reflection) MirrorFocusExempt 0 no, 1 yes Whether nearby and central mirrors skip the capture budget (yes by default). 0 lets the budget slow them too: smoother worst frames, nearby reflections may update less often. Presets keep the map's choice MirrorsOff (no value; launch option only) Turn live reflections off

docs.title: Server cap
docs.text:
Key Limits ?MirrorMaxQuality=<preset name or host asset path> Every value of that preset becomes a limit; only the host needs a custom preset PAK ?MirrorMaxResolution=0.5 Resolution ?MirrorMaxRate=90 Both update rates ?MirrorMaxUpdateRate=90 Normal update rate only ?MirrorMaxFocusRate=144 Focused update rate only ?MirrorMaxDistance=2000 Capture distance (cm) ?MirrorMaxCaptures=3 Captures per frame ?MirrorNoAO Turns reflection AO off ?MirrorNoPartners Turns partnered mirror tunnels off (any ?MirrorMaxQuality= preset except Omega does too) ?MirrorsOff Turns live reflections off

When several limits apply, the strictest wins.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Mirrors render only on players' machines. A dedicated server does no mirror rendering, so hosting costs no GPU. The server shares only the recognized Mirror quality settings listed here with clients; unrelated map options are discarded before replication.
  • Quality is applied when the match starts, and again on your machine if the server's options arrive later.
  • A server's values are applied as the server sets them. A server can choose heavy settings, such as a long capture distance or a high update rate, so only join servers you trust. Your own -MirrorQuality= or single values replace the server's values; only a server cap can lower them.
  • From 0.7.0, Off frees the video memory of the reflections. Mirrors that start Off never reserve it. When Off arrives after the mirrors started (a server's Off reaches you a moment after you join, even if you join mid-match), they switch to dark glass and release it. Mirror stand-ins (the small player copies used in reflections) are not created when mirrors start Off, and stay if Off arrives later; they are cheap. If mirrors are switched back on, the reflections are created again.
